name: James Buchanan
role: President of the United States (1857–1861); earlier senator, secretary of state and diplomat
summary: Buchanan defended a strictly limited federal government and the constitutional protection of slavery while opposing a legal right of secession. He supported territorial expansion and selective economic regulation, alongside fiscal economy and state authority over education.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: He assured Utah residents that changing their faith was their own choice, beyond government interference.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: He opposed borrowing for ordinary expenses and favored expenditure economy; this is not a complete theory of recessions.

collective-defense.rationale: His repeated rejection of entangling alliances with any nation (1842 speech, 1857 letter to Clarendon) is incompatible with a standing pledge to treat an attack on an ally as an attack on all.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He praised protected territorial voting, but backed the minority-supported Lecompton constitution and excluded enslaved people from consent.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: He insisted constitutional judicial rulings protected slave property against contrary territorial legislation.

death-penalty.rationale: In 1837 he said he could not consent to death for any crime but first-degree murder, where the biblical precept applies, and opposed it for arson of public buildings; he accepted execution for the gravest crime but rejected it for terrorism-like offences.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: His homestead veto argued that near-free government farms would demoralize recipients and weaken independence.

decide-locally.rationale: He reserved educational provision to the states and rejected federal college subsidies as unconstitutional consolidation.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He called the 1842 Webster-Ashburton squadron clause an entangling alliance, contrary to Washington's warning, and in 1857 and in instructions to Paraguay he repeated the maxim of avoiding entangling alliances; he did not address troops abroad.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: He praised constitutional rights guarantees against federal abuse and sought similarly binding protection for slavery.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He defended legal ownership of enslaved people and denied extending equal citizenship rights to Black Americans.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: He denied power to wage coercive war against a state, while authorizing defense of federal forts and enforcement of federal law.

free-trade.rationale: In 1844 he called a free trade convention between England and Texas ruinous to American interests, and in 1844 he said America was nearly the only nation where free trade doctrines prevailed, while praising free trade only inside the Union.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: He proposed government-directed settlement and assimilation of Indigenous peoples, subordinating their traditional land control.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: In 1844 he refused to support a memorial asking a 21-year residence before foreigners could enjoy full political privileges and said he opposed any change to the naturalization laws; he said nothing on shorter 'many years' waits.

native-born-offices.rationale: His 1857 inaugural said naturalized citizens are entitled under the Constitution and laws to perfect equality with native-born citizens, and in 1856 he condemned distinctions between citizens born at home or abroad; the constitutional presidential bar is the one limit he did not discuss.

no-business-privileges.rationale: His 1836 letter attacked the rechartered Bank of the United States as a monied monopoly dangerous to liberty and republican institutions and backed Jackson's veto of its charter.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He denied the House supremacy over the executive outside its specific impeachment power.

party-controls-media.rationale: In 1836 and 1839 he said Congress has no power to abridge freedom of the press and called freedom of speech and press the sword and shield of republican institutions; his 1836 bill only withdrew mail protection, it did not control the press.

property-franchise.rationale: In his 1840 Democratic convention speech he called extending the suffrage and abolishing every property qualification a cardinal Democratic principle, because every citizen, rich or poor, is equally entitled to vote.

property-fundamental.rationale: He urged constitutional protection of property claims, including slaveholders’ claims against territorial prohibition.

racial-franchise.rationale: His support for Dred Scott upheld exclusion of people of African descent from national citizenship and political standing.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He demanded stronger bank-charter restrictions, reserve requirements and accountability for paper-money issuance.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: He said government could take no notice whether the Mormons’ creed was true or false and disclaimed control of their ecclesiastical affairs.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He acknowledged the governed’s right to resist oppression, while denying that Lincoln’s election itself justified resistance.

restrict-conversion.rationale: His Utah proclamation allowed believers to retain their religion or change it freely, subject to ordinary law.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: He sought continuing extinguishment of Indigenous title in step with incoming settlement.

right-to-secede.rationale: He denied any constitutional right of unilateral state secession, distinguishing it from revolution.

second-chamber.rationale: In the same 1842 veto speech he argued that a pure numbers argument would equally abolish the Senate and vest all lawmaking in the popular branch, a theory he said experience had exploded.

separated-powers.rationale: He defended the presidency as a coordinate branch independent of ordinary House supervision, subject to constitutional impeachment.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: His postwar account located responsibility chiefly in abolitionist agitation and interference, while acknowledging the slavery dispute throughout.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: He described strict construction of constitutional government powers as the only safe governing rule.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He endorsed incidental manufacturing protection through a revenue tariff and preferred specific duties.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He co-signed the plan to acquire Cuba and continued pursuing annexation and greater regional influence as president.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: In 1836 he warned that vast masses of associated wealth controlled by a single will in the form of legal monopolies are a danger to liberty, with the Bank of the United States as his example.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: He objected to subsidized farms for newly arrived would-be citizens, while insisting naturalized citizens deserve equal treatment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: He sought moderately priced public lands for actual settlers and opposed concentration through speculation.

notes:
No inferred answers. Full annual-message collection, principal domestic vetoes, constitutional protest and 1866 postwar defense were downloaded and searched by theme, with the entire statement list and remaining unknowns checked. Slavery is documented through racial citizenship, unequal legal rights and slave-property protection; it is not automatically equated with land-bound serfdom. His claim that abolitionist agitation caused the rupture is retained as a qualified, low-confidence answer, not adopted as the historical explanation. His later book calls slavery an evil but condemns forcible outside emancipation and does not establish equal political rights. Preserving federal forts is distinguished from coercive war against a state. Neither a personal one-term pledge nor a veto of federal college grants establishes general legal term limits or opposition to tuition-free state colleges. No economic views borrowed from James M. Buchanan. Personal relationships do not establish positions on sexual law. Broad faith, Providence references and constitutional praise do not establish specific church, women’s, ecological or modern technology policies. Native/naturalized equality is not generalized into racial equality. Formal signatures alone are not used; cited proposals and vetoes state his own reasons. General native/naturalized equality does not establish eligibility for every public office, and opposing a homestead immigration incentive does not establish a preferred overall immigration level; both specific statements remain unknown.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 11 answers taken from it, 7 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass from the Senate and congressional record in Moore's Works (vols II, III, IV, V, VI, X), chosen to reach sources different from the first audit's annual messages and vetoes. Themes searched: economy (bank, tariff, public lands), government (veto, suffrage, Senate, press), liberty (free press, death penalty), world (Texas, alliances, trade), society (naturalization, Indians, slavery). Thin on ecology, technology, culture and most social questions: no statements of his own found. Presidential Dec 1860 message and secession positions were not re-read here (volume XI download failed); the first audit covers them. Nothing rests on what a government did apart from his own words or motions. Vol X also holds the inaugural and 1856 letter.
